title: Jihad and Just War Theory
subtitle: The meaning of jihad, its moral limits, and how it compares with Christian just-war thought
summary: Jihad is striving for God and includes moral effort, conveying truth, and regulated armed struggle. It is neither a synonym for terrorism nor exclusively an inward practice. Classical Muslim law also discussed state expansion beyond immediate self-defense, a real point of modern debate. Islam's enduring moral demand is that sacred purpose does not excuse treachery, unlawful targets, or disregard for covenants.

seo.metaTitle: Jihad and Just War Theory: Islamic and Christian Perspectives
seo.metaDescription: Jihad includes moral striving, truth-telling, and lawfully regulated defense. Islam forbids aggression, terrorism, and deliberate attacks on civilians.

sections.title: A Sacred Cause Cannot Make Every Method Sacred
sections.body:
Islam asks human power to answer to God. Jihad means strenuous effort in His service, so an act is not righteous merely because someone gives it a religious name. The cause, authority, intention, targets, and means all matter.

The Quran uses striving for conveying revelation as well as for armed conflict. It is misleading both to translate every jihad as warfare and to deny its genuine military meanings.

sections.title: Spiritual, Moral, and Public Jihad
sections.body:
The authentic basis for moral jihad does not depend on the popular but weakly transmitted slogan about returning from the "lesser" to the "greater" jihad. Jami at-Tirmidhi 1621 records, with a sound grading, that "the mujahid is the one who strives against his own soul." Sunan al-Nasa'i 4209, graded hasan, calls a truthful word before an unjust ruler a form of the best jihad. Surah al-Furqan (25:52) tells the Prophet to strive against rejection through the Quran itself. These sources show that jihad includes spiritual discipline, truth-telling, and conveying revelation.

The Quran also speaks of striving with wealth and person, and of striving against rejection through revelation and patient argument. Context decides which meaning is intended. Translating every occurrence as warfare creates false readings, just as translating every occurrence only as inner spirituality would hide the military sense where it is genuinely present. A trustworthy presentation keeps both meanings and lets the passage determine which applies.

sections.title: The Strong Objection: What About Expansion and Quran 9:29?
sections.body:
Quran 22:39 grounds permission to fight in having been wronged, and 2:190 forbids transgression. But classical warfare doctrine was not limited in every school to repelling an immediate attack. Quran 9:29 and reports such as [Sahih Muslim 1731a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1731a) formed part of broader accounts of state war, conversion invitations, and jizya.

Political submission without forced conversion is not identical to modern religious equality, and historical conquest cannot all be relabeled immediate self-defense. Broader readings of Quran 9:5 also tied release for particular polytheist groups to embracing Islam. The relationship of those readings to the ban on compulsion is a real interpretive issue, not something to conceal.

Contemporary scholars differ over the application of those rulings in a world of citizenship, treaties, and international institutions. Whatever the wider debate, it gives private individuals no right to attack neighbors or travelers. Keeping covenants and avoiding treachery are religious duties, not concessions made because Muslims lack power.

sections.title: The Limits Are Part of the Religious Claim
sections.body:
[Sahih al-Bukhari 3015](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3015) forbids killing women and children. Sahih Muslim 1731a forbids treachery, mutilation, and killing children while addressing military commanders. Even the sources most associated with state warfare place restraints on it.

Classical jurists differed over protected categories and incidental harm; their rules are not identical in every respect to today's terminology of civilians. The distinction must be studied honestly. It cannot be erased by a slogan that everyone of another nationality or religion is an enemy. [Civilian Protection in War](/articles/civilian-protection-in-war) addresses the difficult cases.

sections.title: Compare Traditions at the Same Level
sections.body:
In [Summa Theologiae II-II, question 40](https://www.newadvent.org/summa/3040.htm), Aquinas discusses public authority, just cause, and right intention. Christian just-war reasoning developed further over time. Islamic jurisprudence addresses related questions through its own sources and history.

The comparison should set normative teaching beside normative teaching and historical conduct beside historical conduct. It cannot prove Islam true by comparing Muslim ideals only with Christian atrocities. Islam's positive case is that military power itself remains accountable to God and cannot cancel the duties that govern it.

sections.title: Strive for God Without Giving Anger His Authority
sections.body:
For most readers, jihad begins with truthful speech, discipline, care, learning, generosity, and resistance to injustice through lawful means. Those are serious responsibilities, not lesser substitutes for a dramatic conflict.

Armed struggle brings heavier accountability, not freedom from restraint. Read [Self-Defense in Scripture](/articles/self-defense-in-scripture) for the permission to protect the oppressed, then [Civilian Protection in War](/articles/civilian-protection-in-war) for the limits no cause can simply wish away.

quranVerses.arabic: وَقَٰتِلُوا۟ فِى سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ ٱلَّذِينَ يُقَٰتِلُونَكُمْ وَلَا تَعْتَدُوٓا۟ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يُحِبُّ ٱلْمُعْتَدِينَ
quranVerses.translation: Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you but do not transgress. Indeed. Allah does not like transgressors.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: وَٱقْتُلُوهُمْ حَيْثُ ثَقِفْتُمُوهُمْ وَأَخْرِجُوهُم مِّنْ حَيْثُ أَخْرَجُوكُمْ ۚ وَٱلْفِتْنَةُ أَشَدُّ مِنَ ٱلْقَتْلِ ۚ وَلَا تُقَٰتِلُوهُمْ عِندَ ٱلْمَسْجِدِ ٱلْحَرَامِ حَتَّىٰ يُقَٰتِلُوكُمْ فِيهِ ۖ فَإِن قَٰتَلُوكُمْ فَٱقْتُلُوهُمْ ۗ كَذَٰلِكَ جَزَآءُ ٱلْكَٰفِرِينَ
quranVerses.translation: And kill them wherever you overtake them and expel them from wherever they have expelled you, and fitnah is worse than killing. And do not fight them at al-Masjid al- Haram until they fight you there. But if they fight you, then kill them. Such is the recompense of the disbelievers.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: وَقَٰتِلُوهُمْ حَتَّىٰ لَا تَكُونَ فِتْنَةٌۭ وَيَكُونَ ٱلدِّينُ لِلَّهِ ۖ فَإِنِ ٱنتَهَوْا۟ فَلَا عُدْوَٰنَ إِلَّا عَلَى ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
quranVerses.translation: Fight them until there is no [more] fitnah and [until] worship is [acknowledged to be] for Allah. But if they cease, then there is to be no aggression except against the oppressors.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: أُذِنَ لِلَّذِينَ يُقَٰتَلُونَ بِأَنَّهُمْ ظُلِمُوا۟ ۚ وَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلَىٰ نَصْرِهِمْ لَقَدِيرٌ
quranVerses.translation: Permission [to fight] has been given to those who are being fought, because they were wronged. And indeed, Allah is competent to give them victory.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: فَإِذَا ٱنسَلَخَ ٱلْأَشْهُرُ ٱلْحُرُمُ فَٱقْتُلُوا۟ ٱلْمُشْرِكِينَ حَيْثُ وَجَدتُّمُوهُمْ وَخُذُوهُمْ وَٱحْصُرُوهُمْ وَٱقْعُدُوا۟ لَهُمْ كُلَّ مَرْصَدٍۢ ۚ فَإِن تَابُوا۟ وَأَقَامُوا۟ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَءَاتَوُا۟ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ فَخَلُّوا۟ سَبِيلَهُمْ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَفُورٌۭ رَّحِيمٌۭ
quranVerses.translation: And when the sacred months have passed, then kill the polytheists wherever you find them and capture them and besiege them and sit in wait for them at every place of ambush. But if they should repent, establish prayer, and give zakah, let them [go] on their way. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: قَٰتِلُوا۟ ٱلَّذِينَ لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِٱللَّهِ وَلَا بِٱلْيَوْمِ ٱلْءَاخِرِ وَلَا يُحَرِّمُونَ مَا حَرَّمَ ٱللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُۥ وَلَا يَدِينُونَ دِينَ ٱلْحَقِّ مِنَ ٱلَّذِينَ أُوتُوا۟ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ حَتَّىٰ يُعْطُوا۟ ٱلْجِزْيَةَ عَن يَدٍۢ وَهُمْ صَٰغِرُونَ
quranVerses.translation: Fight those who do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day and who do not consider unlawful what Allah and His Messenger have made unlawful and who do not adopt the religion of truth from those who were given the Scripture - [fight] until they give the jizyah willingly while they are humbled.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: فَلَا تُطِعِ ٱلْكَٰفِرِينَ وَجَٰهِدْهُم بِهِۦ جِهَادًۭا كَبِيرًۭا
quranVerses.translation: So do not obey the disbelievers, and strive against them with the Qur'an a great striving.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: ۞ وَإِن جَنَحُوا۟ لِلسَّلْمِ فَٱجْنَحْ لَهَا وَتَوَكَّلْ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ ۚ إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ ٱلسَّمِيعُ ٱلْعَلِيمُ
quranVerses.translation: And if they incline to peace, then incline to it [also] and rely upon Allah. Indeed, it is He who is the Hearing, the Knowing.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: لَّا يَنْهَىٰكُمُ ٱللَّهُ عَنِ ٱلَّذِينَ لَمْ يُقَٰتِلُوكُمْ فِى ٱلدِّينِ وَلَمْ يُخْرِجُوكُم مِّن دِيَٰرِكُمْ أَن تَبَرُّوهُمْ وَتُقْسِطُوٓا۟ إِلَيْهِمْ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُحِبُّ ٱلْمُقْسِطِينَ
quranVerses.translation: Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you because of religion and do not expel you from your homes - from being righteous toward them and acting justly toward them. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: لَآ إِكْرَاهَ فِى ٱلدِّينِ ۖ قَد تَّبَيَّنَ ٱلرُّشْدُ مِنَ ٱلْغَىِّ ۚ فَمَن يَكْفُرْ بِٱلطَّٰغُوتِ وَيُؤْمِنۢ بِٱللَّهِ فَقَدِ ٱسْتَمْسَكَ بِٱلْعُرْوَةِ ٱلْوُثْقَىٰ لَا ٱنفِصَامَ لَهَا ۗ وَٱللَّهُ سَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ
quranVerses.translation: There shall be no compulsion in [acceptance of] the religion. The right course has become clear from the wrong. So whoever disbelieves in Taghut and believes in Allah has grasped the most trustworthy handhold with no break in it. And Allah is Hearing and Knowing.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

bibleVerses.text: Let every soul be in subjection to the higher authorities, for there is no authority except from God, and those who exist are ordained by God. Therefore he who resists the authority, withstands the ordinance of God; and those who withstand will receive to themselves judgment. For rulers are not a terror to the good work, but to the evil. Do you desire to have no fear of the authority? Do that which is good, and you will have praise from the same, for he is a servant of God to you for good. But if you do that which is evil, be afraid, for he doesn’t bear the sword in vain; for he is a servant of God, an avenger for wrath to him who does evil. Therefore you need to be in subjection, not only because of the wrath, but also for conscience’ sake. For this reason you also pay taxes, for they are servants of God’s service, attending continually on this very thing. Therefore give everyone what you owe: if you owe taxes, pay taxes; if customs, then customs; if respect, then respect; if honor, then honor.
Then he said to them, “But now, whoever has a purse, let him take it, and likewise a wallet. Whoever has none, let him sell his cloak, and buy a sword.
Then Jesus said to him, “Put your sword back into its place, for all those who take the sword will die by the sword.
a time to love, and a time to hate; a time for war, and a time for peace.

But of the cities of these peoples, that Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance, you shall save alive nothing that breathes; but you shall utterly destroy them: the Hittite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite; as Yahweh your God has commanded you; that they not teach you to follow all their abominations, which they have done to their gods; so would you sin against Yahweh your God.

Therefore subject yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord’s sake: whether to the king, as supreme; or to governors, as sent by him for vengeance on evildoers and for praise to those who do well.

faq.question: Does jihad simply mean holy war?
faq.answer: No. It means striving for God and can concern self-discipline, conveying truth, service, or armed struggle. Nor does it mean only inward effort: the military sense is real in its proper contexts.

faq.question: Is the statement about greater and lesser jihad authentic?
faq.answer: The popular wording about returning from lesser to greater jihad has a weak chain. The importance of striving against the self is established independently in Jami at-Tirmidhi 1621, graded sound.

faq.question: Can jihad be used to force conversion?
faq.answer: Quran 2:256 rejects compulsion in religion, but some classical readings of Quran 9:5 also allowed an ultimatum of accepting Islam or continued warfare for particular polytheist groups. Describing that solely as political submission would conceal a real difficulty. Scholars differ over the scope of those rules and their relationship to the ban on compulsion. That debate gives individuals no permission to attack people or force a profession of faith.

faq.question: Does Islam permit terrorism?
faq.answer: Attacks on protected people, treachery, and private violence cannot be made lawful by calling them jihad. A state's authorization also does not automatically make its targets or methods righteous. The cause and conduct must meet the relevant moral and legal duties.

furtherReading.title: When God Says War Is Right: The Christian's Perspective on When and How to Fight
furtherReading.author: Darrell M. Cole
furtherReading.note: Accessible overview of Christian Just War thinking, relating the tradition to Romans 13 and applying it to modern conflicts, including a post-9/11 comparison with Islamic just-war reasoning.

furtherReading.title: Arguing the Just War in Islam
furtherReading.author: John Kelsay
furtherReading.note: Scholarly study (Harvard University Press, 2007) of the shari'a-based jurisprudential tradition on war, tracing how classical and contemporary Muslim jurists have argued over the legitimacy and limits of armed conflict.

furtherReading.title: Fiqh al-Jihad ("The Jurisprudence of Jihad: A Comparative Study of Its Rulings and Philosophy in Light of the Quran and Sunnah")
furtherReading.author: Yusuf al-Qaradawi
furtherReading.note: A major two-volume contemporary Islamic legal study (published in Arabic, 2009) arguing for a defensive, restrictive reading of the rules of jihad and against the targeting of civilians, grounded in detailed jurisprudential sources.

furtherReading.title: Just Wars, Holy Wars, and Jihads: Christian, Jewish, and Muslim Encounters and Exchanges
furtherReading.author: Sohail H. Hashmi (editor)
furtherReading.note: Edited volume (Oxford University Press, 2012) comparing Christian, Jewish, and Muslim traditions of ethical reasoning about war across history, from the early Islamic conquests to the present.
